newsitem.title: GERMANY: Half German voters want softer EMU criteria - poll.
newsitem.headline: Half German voters want softer EMU criteria - poll.

text.p: More than half of German voters want the strict economic criteria to qualify for Europe's planned single currency to be softened and only one-fifth think they should be applied strictly, according to a new opinion poll.

The survey by the respected Allensbach Institute also said 47.6 percent of the sample group opposed the euro, the new currency planned for 1999, while 41.6 percent said they supported it. Only 10.8 percent were undecided.

On the criteria, 55.2 percent said they should be softened, while 19.6 percent wanted to see them applied as laid down in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, according to the poll reported by Bavarian Television on Wednesday evening.
One-quarter -- 25.2 percent -- of those questioned were unsure how the criteria should be applied, the poll found.

Asked about the euro's effect on unemployment in Germany, 39.7 percent said it would make the problem worse, while only 7.8 percent thought the single currency would help fight job losses. The largest group -- 40.9 percent -- expected no change and 11.6 percent were undecided.
The poll also showed widespread scepticism about the savings plans Bonn has drawn up to help it trim spending to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

A full 55.3 percent said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition was being too tough in cutting spending and 86.7 percent said the cuts were not fair. The survey did not ask for reactions to specific austerity plans Bonn has proposed.
The Maastricht criteria set two ceilings for EMU members -- a budget deficit of three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) and national debt at or below 60 percent of GDP.
